question.text: Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are two events such that $P(A)=0.45,$ $P(B)=0.35,$ and $P(A\cap B)=0.3,$ find $P(A\cup B).$
question.explanation:
The addition law for probability states that

\[ P(A\cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A\cap B). \]

So, to calculate $P(A\cup B),$ we apply the addition law: \[ \begin{align*} P(A\cup B) &= P(A) + P(B) - P(A\cap B)\\[5pt] &= 0.45 + 0.35 - 0.3\\[5pt] &= 0.5 \end{align*} \]

exampleAnswers.title: Applying the Addition Law in Context

question.text: John selected a pair of socks out of his drawer without looking in the drawer. He has $5$ pairs of black dress socks, $4$ pairs of brown dress socks, $10$ pairs of black sports socks, and $3$ pairs of white sport socks. What is the probability of selecting a pair of black socks or a pair of sports socks?
question.explanation:
Let us call $B$ the event "a pair of black socks has been selected," and $S$ the event "a pair of sports socks has been selected." Then the probability of selecting a pair of black socks or a pair of sports socks is $P(B\cup S),$ and we can apply the addition law:

\[\eqalign{ P(B\cup S)=P(B)+P(S)-P(B\cap S) }\]

First, let's find $P(B),$ $P(S),$ and $P(B \cap S).$

  • There are $5+10=15$ pairs of black socks among the $5+4+10+3=22$ pairs of socks, so we have \[ P(B) = \dfrac{15}{22}. \]

  • There are $10+3=13$ pairs of sports socks among the $22$ pairs of socks, so we have \[ P(S) = \dfrac{13}{22}. \]

  • There are $10$ pairs of black sports socks. So, we have \[ P(B \cap S) = \dfrac{10}{22}. \]

Therefore, applying the addition law, we have

\[\eqalign{ P(B\cup S)&=P(B)+P(S)-P(B\cap S) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{15}{22}+\dfrac{13}{22}-\dfrac{10}{22} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{18}{22}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{9}{11}. }\]

question.text: A fair spinner with $15$ equal sectors is labeled with the numbers $1$ through $15.$ What is the probability of getting a prime number or an even number after launching the spinner?
question.explanation:
Let us call $R$ the event "we get a prime number," and $E$ the event "we get an even number." Then the probability of getting a prime number or an even number is $P(R \cup E),$ and we can apply the addition law:

\[ \begin{align*} P(R\cup E) &= P(R) + P(E) - P(R\cap E) \end{align*} \]

First, let's find $P(R),$ $P(E),$ and $P(R \cap E).$

  • There are $6$ prime numbers among the $15$ labels of the spinner ($2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13$), so we have \[ P(R) = \frac{6}{15}. \]

  • There are $7$ even numbers among the $15$ labels of the spinner ($2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14$), so we have \[ P(E) = \frac{7}{15}. \]

  • There is only a single number, $2,$ that is both prime and even. So, we have \[ P(R \cap E) = \frac{1}{15}. \]

Therefore, applying the addition law, we have

\[ \begin{align*} P(R\cup E) &= P(R) + P(E) - P(R\cap E)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{6}{15} + \dfrac{7}{15} - \dfrac{1}{15}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4}{5}. \end{align*} \]

question.text:
A card is drawn at random from a standard $52$-card deck. What is the probability of drawing a number card greater than $7$ or a non-spade card?

Hint: A standard $52$-card pack has four suits, each containing $13$ cards. Spades is one of these suits. Number cards are the cards labelled $2$ through $10$ in each suit. A jack, queen or king is not considered a number card.
question.explanation:
Let's call $G$ the event "a card labeled with a number greater than $7$ is selected" and $N$ the event "a non-spade card is selected."

The required probability is $P(G \cup N),$ which we can find using the addition law \[ P(G \cup N) = P(G) + P(N) - P(G \cap N). \]

Let's find $P(G)$ and $P(N).$

  • There are $12$ cards labeled with a number greater than $7$ in a standard deck. So, we have \[ P(G) = \dfrac{12}{52} = \dfrac{3}{13}. \]

  • There are $39$ non-spade cards in a standard deck. So, we have \[ P(N) = \dfrac{39}{52} = \dfrac{3}{4}. \]

  • There are $9$ non-spade cards labeled with a number greater than $7.$ Indeed, the cards labeled with a number greater than $7$ are $8,$ $9,$ and $10,$ giving $3$ such cards per suit. Since there are $3$ non-spade suits, we have

\[ P(G \cap N)=\dfrac{9}{52}. \]

Finally, substituting all of the known information into the addition law, we get \begin{align*} P(G \cup N) & = P(G) + P(N) - P(G \cap N) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{3}{13} + \dfrac{3}{4} - \dfrac{9}{52}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{21}{26}. \end{align*}

question.text:
A card is drawn at random from a standard $52$-card deck. What is the probability of drawing a card labeled with a number less than $4$ or a spade card?

*Hint: A standard $52$-card deck has $4$ suits with $13$ cards in each suit. Spades is one of the suits. Number cards are the cards labeled $2$ through $10$ in each suit.
question.explanation:
Let's call $A$ the event "a card labeled with a number less than $4$ is selected" and $B$ the event "a spade card is selected."

The required probability is $P(A \cup B),$ which we can find using the addition law \[ P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B). \]

Let's find $P(A)$ and $P(B).$

  • There are $2\cdot 4 = 8$ cards labeled with a number less than $4$ in a standard deck. So, we have \[ P(A) = \dfrac{8}{52} = \dfrac{2}{13}. \]

  • There are $13$ spade cards in a standard deck. So, we have \[ P(B) = \dfrac{13}{52} = \dfrac{1}{4}. \]

  • There are $2$ spade cards labeled with a number less than $4$ (the $2$ of spades and the $3$ of spades). Therefore,

\[ P(A \cap B)=\dfrac{2}{52}=\dfrac{1}{26}. \]

Finally, substituting all of the known information into the addition law, we get \begin{align*} P(A \cup B) & = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2}{13} + \dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{26} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{19}{52}. \end{align*}
